_note: Plain-language glossary. Groups are 'title|icon-id'; each term is [term, also known as, definition, stage slug]. Used by glossary.html and by site.js for in-text definitions on stage pages.

Places and institutions|d-plan: A regional state in north-western and central Ethiopia, largely highland, and the setting of the pilot.
An administrative level below the region, for example a zone in Gojjam, Gondar, Wollo or Shewa.
An administrative district. The pilot starts in one woreda.
The smallest administrative unit, a rural community. Pilot data are reported by kebele.
A kebele-level extension worker who advises farmers and, in this system, records field operations.
A kebele facility for demonstrations and training.
A farmers' cooperative at kebele level that buys inputs and sells produce for its members.
A federation of primary cooperatives that supplies inputs at scale and sells to large buyers.
A group of irrigators that shares and manages water from a scheme or river.
A document recording a household's right to use a plot. Land is not bought or sold; plans work with these rights.
Seasons and climate|i-03: The main rainy season, roughly June to September, that feeds the Meher crop.
The short rainy season, roughly February to May, and the crops grown in it in Belg areas.
The dry season, roughly October to January, when irrigation matters most.
The main cropping season, rain-fed by Kiremt, planted around mid-year and harvested from about October.
The first planting rain that is not followed by a long dry spell: here, 20 mm in 3 days with no 7-day dry spell in the next 30 days.
Rain that looks like the season starting but is followed by a long dry spell, which can kill seedlings.
A run of days with almost no rain; most harmful in the weeks after planting.
How unusual a season's rainfall is compared with the long-term record; -1 or below marks a drought year.
How temperature falls with altitude, about 6.5 °C per kilometre; used to estimate frost risk higher up.
The water a reference grass would use in a day, driven by heat and sunshine.
How much more or less water a crop uses than the reference grass at each growth stage.
The part of the rain a crop can actually use; the rest runs off or drains away.
Water deliberately left in a river so that it stays healthy for people and nature downstream.
Water that refills an aquifer each year; only a share of it should be pumped.
Land and crops|i-01: A tiny-grained cereal native to Ethiopia, the staple for injera; tolerant of waterlogged soils but shatters easily when over-ripe.
A flat-topped highland mountain, typical of the northern Ethiopian landscape.
A traditional round house with a conical roof.
A heavy black clay soil that swells when wet and can waterlog in the main rains.
A levelled step on a slope that slows erosion and keeps soil and water in place.
Highly, moderately and marginally suitable, and not suitable, for a crop on a piece of land.
The land quality that holds suitability down, for example acidic soil or steep slope.
A way to turn expert pairwise judgements into weights, with a check that they are consistent.
A satellite measure of how green and dense vegetation is; it rises as a crop grows and falls as it matures.
A pair of European satellites that image the land about every five days at 10 to 20 m detail.
Harvesting and weighing a small marked area of a field to measure yield.
Planning and markets|i-05: A group of neighbouring plots planned together so that volumes are large enough for buyers.
A mathematical method that finds the best plan within limits such as land, water and demand.
How much extra income one more unit of a limited resource would bring, for example one more cubic metre of water in March.
What buyers will take: a contracted minimum, an absorbable maximum and a planning price.
A pre-season agreement with a buyer on volume, grade, delivery month and how the price is set.
A contract price that follows the market but never goes below a floor or above a ceiling.
Selling contracted produce to someone else because they pay more at harvest.
How prices in each month usually compare with the yearly average, after removing inflation.
Operations|i-11: The time between placing an order and receiving it; it varies, so plans use its 90th percentile.
The latest date to order an input so it arrives before it is needed in 9 cases out of 10.
The share of planned field operations done within their time window.
Harvesting first the plots whose ripeness window closes soonest, to cut field losses.
A batch of grain with an ID that lists the plots it came from, so quality and payment can be traced.
An airtight storage bag that starves insects of oxygen, keeping storage losses very low.
A record that a farmer group owns a graded lot in store; it can back a loan or a later sale.
A store where small lots from many plots are combined into buyer-sized volumes.
A method to choose where to put a number of centres so that total haul distance is as short as possible.
A route-planning method that merges trips whose combination saves the most distance, filling trucks.
Evaluation and learning|u-loop: Surveys before and after the pilot that measure the same things in the same households.
A similar kebele outside the pilot, used to see what would have happened anyway.
Impact = change in pilot households minus change in comparison households; removes inflation and weather.
A lesson sent back up the chain after each season, such as realised yields per suitability class.
Generated, made-up data used in demos to show how methods behave; never real farmers or places.
A code such as HH-0001 used instead of a person's name, so records can be linked without identifying anyone.
